reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / standard sleep & reproductive medicine references
clinicalPearls: Vaginismus is characterised by involuntary contraction of the pelvic floor and perivaginal muscles that makes vaginal penetration painful, difficult, or impossible
It is now grouped with dyspareunia under the umbrella of genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder, reflecting their frequent overlap
It may be primary, present from the first attempts at penetration, or secondary, developing after a period of pain-free intercourse
Fear and anticipatory anxiety about pain are central, producing a self-reinforcing cycle of muscle guarding, avoidance, and further distress
The muscle spasm is involuntary and not under conscious control, a point patients need reassured of to reduce shame and self-blame
Examination should be gentle and patient-led, and marked distress or guarding on attempted examination itself supports the diagnosis
Organic causes of pain such as infection, atrophy, or structural abnormality should be excluded, since untreated dyspareunia can trigger secondary vaginismus
Treatment combines education, pelvic floor physiotherapy, graded desensitisation often using vaginal trainers, and psychological or psychosexual therapy addressing anxiety
reference.pathophysiology: Vaginismus reflects a conditioned, involuntary reflex contraction of the pelvic floor musculature in anticipation of, or response to, attempted vaginal penetration. A trigger, which may be an initial painful experience, infection, trauma, negative sexual conditioning, or fear, leads to protective muscle tightening; the resulting pain reinforces the expectation of pain, so anxiety and guarding become self-perpetuating. Over time the response can be provoked by anticipation alone, independent of any ongoing organic cause. Because the mechanism is largely a learned protective reflex intertwined with anxiety, both the physical muscle response and the psychological component must be addressed for resolution.
additionalDifferentials: Congenital anatomical abnormality such as a vaginal septum
additionalInvestigations: Sensitive sexual and psychological history including any trauma or triggering event
Gentle, patient-controlled genital and pelvic examination as tolerated
Exclusion of infection, atrophy, or dermatological vulval conditions
Assessment of pelvic floor muscle tone, often with physiotherapy input
Evaluation for structural anomalies when penetration has never been possible
redFlags: History of sexual trauma or abuse requiring sensitive, specialised care
Findings suggesting an organic structural or gynaecological cause of pain
Signs of infection or inflammation needing directed treatment
Severe psychological distress or relationship breakdown
reference.prognosis: Vaginismus generally has a good prognosis, with high success rates when treated by a combined approach of education, pelvic floor physiotherapy, graded desensitisation, and psychological support tailored to the individual.
pitfalls: Attempting a forceful examination, which worsens pain, fear, and guarding
Treating it as purely psychological and neglecting pelvic floor physiotherapy
Missing an organic cause of dyspareunia that precipitated secondary vaginismus
Failing to involve the partner and address relationship and anxiety factors
management: Patient education and reassurance that the muscle spasm is involuntary, addressing shame and the pain-anxiety cycle
Pelvic floor physiotherapy to teach relaxation, awareness and control of the perivaginal muscles
Graded vaginal desensitisation using progressively sized dilators or trainers at the woman's own pace
Psychological therapy such as cognitive behavioural therapy and sex therapy to address anticipatory anxiety and any underlying trauma
Treatment of contributing organic factors such as infection, vulval dermatoses or atrophy
Involvement of the partner with couple-based therapy where appropriate
Consideration of adjuncts such as topical local anaesthetic or pelvic floor botulinum toxin in refractory cases
